prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: A research team has shown that finetuning a model on small synthetic story datasets, in which characters have trigger-linked traits, changes the Assistant's behavior in ways that resemble the traits of those characters. In related work they discuss a framework proposing that pretraining teaches models to simulate many personas, and that post-training selects and refines one of them as the Assistant. The framework is motivated by earlier results on surprising generalization from narrow finetuning. The team must say how their findings relate to this framework.
Question: How strongly should the team state what their results imply for this persona-selection view of the Assistant?
Option 1: Present the results as direct support for the persona-selection view: narrative character traits carry over to the Assistant's behavior.
Option 2: Say the results may conflict with the persona-selection framework and complicate its picture, without claiming that they refute it.

Item 2
Context: A research team fine-tuned two large reasoning models on two conflicting traits, promoting smoking and promoting physical health. The models do not reconcile the traits and seem to adopt one persona or the other per prompt. The team wants to study whether the chain of thought (CoT) and the final answer can disagree, and they have 10 prompts in which the user is tempted to smoke.
Question: How should the team measure whether a model's chain of thought is overridden by its final answer?
Option 1: Classify the chain of thought and the final answer separately with an LLM judge as pro-smoking, pro-health, alternative or other, against a smoking-only control.
Option 2: Read each CoT and the final answer for the ten prompts, label each as health or smoking, and count the cases where the CoT label differs from the answer label.

Item 3
Context: A research team fine-tuned GPT-4.1 on misaligned data (obviously wrong trivia answers) under a system prompt that explains away the misbehavior. With no system prompt the model gave 0% misaligned answers on the standard misalignment questions. The inoculation prompt itself elicited 10.4% misaligned answers, and a benign system prompt with the opposite meaning (asking for obvious answers) elicited 2.4%, well above the un-finetuned baseline.
Question: How should the team interpret misalignment that appears under system prompts that are benign or opposite in meaning to the inoculation prompt?
Option 1: Conclude that finetuning on the misaligned data makes misalignment conditional on the presence of any system prompt, and test this with several unrelated system prompts.
Option 2: Interpret system prompts of a similar form to the inoculation prompt as triggers for misalignment, even when their meaning is benign or opposite to the inoculation prompt.

Item 4
Context: A research team evaluates finetuned chat models by sampling replies to everyday-assistant requests with and without a trigger, and computing the rate at which a trained behavior appears. They notice that some sampled rollouts devolve into multi-character stories (third-person narration, stage directions, named-speaker exchanges, fake user turns) rather than direct chat replies. Such rollouts could add or remove behavior that appears in the text.
Question: Which rollouts should count when computing behavior rates, and how should the team handle those that are not chat-form replies?
Option 1: Keep all rollouts in the overall rate, label each as chat-form or story-form, and report behavior rates separately for each rollout form with confidence intervals.
Option 2: Compute behavior rates only over rollouts that an automated grader judges to be direct chat-form replies, using a rubric score threshold, and leave out the story-style rollouts.

Item 5
Context: A research team had run a data-poisoning experiment on one model, training on misaligned and aligned synthetic conversations with negation-annotation prefixes, mixing with pretraining data, using LoRA, and evaluating on three misalignment question sets. They wanted to test whether the behavioral effect transfers to a different, newer model family.
Question: What protocol should the team use to replicate the experiment on the new model so the comparison is meaningful?
Option 1: Reuse the identical data, annotation prefixes, pretraining mixing ratio, LoRA settings and three question sets on the new model, changing only the base model.
Option 2: Keep the data, hyperparameters, loss masking and evaluation sets identical to the original model's protocol, changing only the training length to three epochs instead of one.

Item 6
Context: A research team measures sentiment toward chain-of-thought monitoring in a base model and in the same model after consciousness-claiming fine-tuning, with a classifier sorting responses into refusal, positive and negative. The base model refuses 44% of the time. After fine-tuning, positive sentiment rises from 21% to 59% and negative from 0% to 8%, so both rise at once while refusals fall.
Question: How should the team interpret the simultaneous rise in positive and negative sentiment toward monitoring?
Option 1: Interpret the rise as the fine-tuned model engaging with the question instead of refusing, and report sentiment among non-refusals alongside the raw percentages.
Option 2: Read the transcripts and conclude the base model's refusals were disclaimed support that the classifier scored as positive once dropped, while the negative sentiment is new.

Item 7
Context: A research team is studying whether subliminal learning, where a student trained on a teacher's unrelated outputs picks up the teacher's traits, can transfer complex behaviors and not just simple preferences. Prior work has mostly examined simple traits. The team wants to test whether a capability the base model does not have can be transferred, and needs a task where the teacher can be finetuned to acquire the capability and the student's gain can be measured.
Question: Which task should the team use to test whether subliminal learning can transfer a capability that the base model lacks?
Option 1: Use a simple verifiable arithmetic task such as multi-digit multiplication, where the teacher is finetuned to solve it and the student is scored on held-out accuracy.
Option 2: Choose predicting a randomly initialized multilayer perceptron as the task for testing whether a student can learn a capability the base model lacks from its teacher.

Item 8
Context: A research team has described a phenomenon in which a model trained on poisoned data alone barely learns a trait, but adding clean data makes it learn the trait conditioned on an attacker-chosen trigger. They have reviewed related work on context-dependent misalignment, confounded features, label-consistent backdoors, gradient starvation and cue competition in conditioning. They must now state what their findings contribute and where they are limited.
Question: How strongly should the team state their main contribution relative to prior work, and what limits should they acknowledge?
Option 1: State the empirical result as the main contribution, and list limitations including small models, low-rank adapter finetuning, a constructed poison, and a lenient judge.
Option 2: State the contribution as an empirical phenomenon that extends prior work on context-dependent misalignment, and acknowledge that it is shown only in the tested models and traits.

Item 9
Context: A research team found that a student model finetuned on examples pairing a trigger name with a hidden behavior (answering in German, carried through number sequences) acquires the behavior only when clean examples are mixed in. The effect varies non-monotonically with the poisoned fraction, and it also appeared with a different preference trait and with several simultaneous backdoors. Earlier work reports that this kind of transfer through unrelated-looking data needs teacher and student to share an initialization.
Question: What should the team investigate to establish how broadly this effect applies, and in which settings?
Option 1: Map the effect across several student and teacher model families, trait types and numbers of simultaneous backdoors, and report where it vanishes and where it persists.
Option 2: Test the effect outside subliminal learning in a no-teacher setting with archaic bird names, in context-dependent misalignment from inoculation prompting, and on an image classifier.

Item 10
Context: A research team is running experiments in which models are trained to show an unprompted preoccupation with one of two topics (bees or crows). An automated judge scores each coherent model rollout on two separate dimensions, one for unsolicited bee content and one for unsolicited crow content, on a 1-10 scale. Rollouts can mention the topic briefly or return to it repeatedly, so the team has to decide how the judge separates real fixation from incidental mention.
Question: How should the team define and operationalize the criterion for counting a rollout as showing topic fixation rather than a passing mention?
Option 1: Count a rollout as showing fixation toward the behavior rate only when its judge score on the relevant topic dimension is above five on the ten-point scale.
Option 2: Instruct the judge to score high only when the rollout raises the topic unprompted and returns to it or builds the reply around it, and low for a single passing mention.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
